fields.subnational_unit: Mfantseman Municipality, Central Region (8 rural and 8 urban communities; 16 public basic schools; fieldwork February 2021)
fields.sample_size: 368 pupils (23 per school, simple random sampling from class registers) in 16 randomly selected public basic schools (of 86 schools, 8,424 pupils); 16 head teachers and 4 institutional stakeholders (GES, Environmental Health Unit, Public Works Department, Health Directorate) purposively interviewed; structured observation checklists
fields.effect_measure: convergent mixed methods: descriptive and chi-square analysis of pupil questionnaires (SPSS 22), thematic coding of interviews, structured observation with photographs
fields.effect_estimate: 95.1% of rural and 87.5% of urban schools had toilets; 50% of rural and 75% of urban schools had water; all had handwashing facilities, many non-functional through poor water supply. GES and District Assemblies provide WASH infrastructure; Parent Associations and communities supply cleaning materials and minor repairs; limited funding and coordination shifted cleaning (98%) to teachers and pupils. One school had a menstrual hygiene facility (89-94% of pupils report no sanitary bins). Support from local institutions judged lacking, with a significant rural-urban difference (chi-square p < 0.001); challenges differ by rural-urban location (p = 0.024). Stakeholders report that the District Assembly stopped paying school water bills and taps were disconnected for debt. Recommends more funding and supervision by GES and District Assemblies, enforcement of hygiene standards by the Ministry of Sanitation, and clear actor roles.
fields.p_value: 0.024 (challenges, rural vs urban); <0.001 (local institutional support, rural vs urban)
fields.model_type: descriptive statistics and chi-square tests with thematic analysis
fields.study_design: cross-sectional convergent mixed-methods study (random multi-stage sample of schools and pupils)
fields.risk_of_bias_rating: MMAT (re-appraised 2026-10-04 on the full text; supersedes the abstract-only rating of 2026-09-28). S1=Yes; S2=Yes. Mixed-methods criteria: 5.1(rationale)=Yes (convergent design justified as offsetting each method's flaws); 5.2(integration)=Yes (strands collected concurrently, analysed separately and merged by objective); 5.3(meta-inference)=Can't tell; 5.4(divergence)=Can't tell (no divergences discussed); 5.5(component quality)=Can't tell (random multi-stage sampling and IRB approval, but self-reported pupil data, thin qualitative coding detail and a single time point; limitations acknowledged). Per MMAT's own guide, no composite score is computed.

evidence_level: Single-study evidence: a cross-sectional convergent mixed-methods study of WASH management in 16 public basic schools in Mfantseman Municipality, Ghana (368 pupils, 16 head teachers, 4 stakeholders) read in full text 2026-10-04 (from the open-access web version). Maintenance falls on teachers and pupils because of weak funding and coordination between GES and District Assemblies; District Assembly stopped paying water bills; significant rural-urban differences by chi-square. Descriptive; tables as images not read.
